items.followUp: Define boiling and state two factors that affect the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: Identifies evaporation as a surface process in which a liquid changes into vapour below its boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the essential definition: a liquid changes into vapour from its surface below its boiling point.

rubric.why: Higher temperature gives liquid particles more energy, increasing the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing temperature increases the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: A larger exposed surface allows more liquid particles to escape at a time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing surface area increases the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: Moving air carries away vapour, while lower humidity allows more vapour to enter the air.
rubric.description: Effect of wind speed or humidity
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that faster wind or lower humidity increases evaporation.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface at a temperature below its boiling point.
An increase in temperature increases the rate of evaporation because more particles have enough energy to escape.
An increase in the exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
A higher wind speed increases evaporation by carrying vapour away; lower humidity also increases evaporation.

items.followUp: Define a homogeneous mixture and give one example.

rubric.why: A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition, so its components are not distributed evenly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the composition is non-uniform or that the components are not evenly distributed.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates a mixture with distinguishable or unevenly distributed components.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example, such as sand and water.

modelAnswer: A heterogeneous mixture is a mixture whose composition is not uniform throughout and whose components can be distinguished.

items.followUp: Write the empirical and molecular formulae of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆.

rubric.why: The simplest whole-number ratio of carbon to hydrogen in benzene is 1:1.
Benzene contains six carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms per molecule.

items.followUp: Define a molecule and give an example of a diatomic molecule.

rubric.why: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retains its chemical properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a molecule as the smallest independently existing particle of an element or compound that retains its properties.

rubric.why: Each example contains three atoms in one molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid triatomic example, such as H₂O, O₃, or CO₂.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of an element or compound that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
Water, H₂O, is an example of a triatomic molecule.

items.followUp: State one limitation of Rutherford’s atomic model and explain it briefly.

rubric.why: According to classical theory, orbiting electrons should continuously lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, so the model could not explain atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford’s model could not explain why electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus.

rubric.why: The model did not specify how electrons are arranged around the nucleus and could not explain atomic line spectra.
rubric.description: Failure to explain electron arrangement or line spectra
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another valid defect, such as failure to explain electron arrangement or line spectra.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of an atom: revolving electrons should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
It did not explain the arrangement of electrons around the nucleus or the line spectra of atoms.

items.followUp: An element has atomic number 12. Write the number of electrons in its K, L and M shells.

rubric.why: The first shell is filled with two electrons before electrons enter the next shell.
The remaining electrons are distributed as 8 in the L shell and 7 in the M shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both L = 8 and M = 7.

modelAnswer: For a neutral atom, number of electrons = atomic number = 17.
K shell = 2 electrons; L shell = 8 electrons; M shell = 7 electrons.

items.followUp: What are alkali metals? Give one example.

rubric.why: Transition metals are commonly identified by partially filled d subshells in their atoms or ions, and are found in groups 3 to 12.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying transition metals by incomplete d subshells or their position in groups 3–12.

rubric.why: Iron, copper and chromium are examples of transition metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example, such as iron or copper.

modelAnswer: Transition metals are elements whose atoms or common ions have partially filled d-orbitals; they are found in groups 3 to 12 of the periodic table.

items.followUp: Define electron affinity and write an equation showing the electron affinity of chlorine.

rubric.why: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom, forming a positive ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as the energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.

rubric.why: The sodium example shows removal of an electron to form a positive gaseous ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as Na(g) + energy → Na⁺(g) + e⁻.

modelAnswer: Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom to form a positive ion.
